topic: The Attention Mechanism: How Transformers Read
target_audience: University students with basic programming/linear algebra knowledge

sections.title: The Problem: Information Overload
sections.content: Introduce the limitation of previous models (RNNs) which struggle with long-range dependencies. Define 'Attention' as the ability to selectively focus on relevant parts of input.
sections.example: Reading a long mystery novel: You don't memorize every word; you focus on the clues that link the detective to the culprit.

sections.title: The Core Components: Query, Key, and Value
sections.content: Explain the Q, K, V retrieval system using an analogy to a library database. Visual: Query (what I want), Key (the labels on the book spines), Value (the content inside).
sections.example: A library search: Your search term (Query) is compared against book titles (Keys) to retrieve the most useful information (Values).

sections.title: Calculating Relevance: Dot Product & Softmax
sections.content: Introduce the mathematical intuition: Score = (Query · Key) / sqrt(d). Use a heat map graphic to show how similar items get higher weights, then 'Softmax' turns these into probabilities (percentages).
sections.example: Visualizing a 'focus matrix': If the word is 'Apple', the matrix shows a bright 'red' spot on 'fruit' and a 'dim' spot on 'jump'.

sections.title: Bringing it Together: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
sections.content: Combine the concepts: Multiply the weights by the Values to get a 'weighted sum.' This is the final vector representation that the model 'understands'.
sections.example: Imagine a chef choosing ingredients: The weight (Attention) determines how much salt or spice (Value) goes into the final dish based on the recipe (Query).

sections.title: Application: Multi-Head Attention
sections.content: Explain that Transformers run multiple 'attention' processes in parallel to capture different types of relationships simultaneously (grammar, sentiment, context).
sections.example: A team of researchers: One person focuses on the historical facts, another on the emotional tone, and a third on the scientific logic—all synthesizing one final summary.
